title: Boggle and the Moonbeam Friend
markdown:
The peaks of the Ashlands are not gentle. They are sharp proud teeth of stone against a sky that always seems twilight. Fiery breath of sleeping volcanoes has cooled into meadows of soft grey ash. Warm mineral springs bubble near veins of black basalt. Goblins live in dwellings dug into the slopes.

Among them was Boggle, a goblin of considerable cleverness, tunic a little more patched than perfect. His true treasure was Moss, a ferret of remarkable shininess, coat the colour of a rusty sunset, a flash of loyal quickness against the stark landscape.

One particularly crisp dawn, air still sharp, black rocks gleaming with dew, Boggle had a simple mission: shimmering moss that mended and brightened, growing only in the deep cool shadows of the Whispering Crags, enough to patch his roof. Moss trotted ahead, sensitive nose twitching, a tiny furry explorer.

As Boggle rounded a sharp craggy bend, Moss froze, a taut still line. Boggle followed his gaze. Nestled in a sun-warmed patch of ash, a place usually as bare as a winter branch, was a creature unlike any he had met.

Small as a plump well-fed mushroom, spun from night sky: starlight and threads of pure moonlight, large dark eyes blinking slow. As it moved it shimmered, casting faint dreamy patterns on grey dust. Boggle knew it was wonder, and quite lost.

His heart, often focused on practical moss-patching, was as soft as the moss itself was useful. He could not leave this small delicate light. With a sigh that ruffled his pointed ears he gathered the shimmering creature. It felt like holding captured moonlight, cool and comforting. Moss led not toward the Whispering Crags but toward the bustling heart of the Ashlands: The Smoldering Kettle Inn.

The Smoldering Kettle Inn, you must understand if you have never been, smelled of steam and stew and a hundred kinds of busy. Chimneys puffed cheerful white plumes against twilight. Boggle had meant to sit in a corner with Glimmer until the roof-moss errand could resume. Glimmer’s light made even the steam look kinder. Moss, usually restless, sat as still as he had on the ash patch, watching the inn the way he watched a new scent: thoroughly, without hurry. Instead the inn handed Boggle three knots at once, as inns will, and Moss’s nose began its quiet work.

Griselda the innkeeper, considerable size, voice to rival rumbling earth, was beside herself. “My prize-winning Cinderbloom Stew. Vanished.” She pointed at Niamh the Baker, a round goblin whose nose seemed perpetually dusted with flour. Niamh sputtered like a damp firecracker. “I only took a small taste. A mere tiny taste.” Just then a large contented mountain marmot, whiskers with a reddish smear, waddled from a steaming cauldron, belly suspiciously round.

Next: traveling gnomes, renowned for clockwork instruments. Lead fiddler Pipkin, hat of tiny spinning gears, wailed that his Lumina-Fiddle had been stolen. “It glows in the dark. Utterly unique.” Eyes drifted toward Reginald, a smartly dressed goblin merchant nervously polishing a shiny, faintly glowing fiddle case. “I merely borrowed it to admire its craftsmanship. A momentary lapse.”

Third: every few minutes heavy copper pots jiggled and hopped across the stone, clattering as if possessed by a jig. Mort the cook, surly but secretly kind, was convinced of a poltergeist. “They’ve never done this before.” He lunged after a runaway saucepan.

Boggle had meant to find a quiet corner. Instead he noticed Moss sniffing Niamh’s flour-dusted apron, a glint of understanding in beady ferret eyes. The star-spun creature in his arms — he thought of it as Glimmer — gazed at Reginald’s case, its own ethereal glow pulsating as if in gentle resonance. And beneath the floorboards, a subtle rhythmic thrumming, almost mechanical.

Boggle nudged Moss. Moss launched, ferret-fast, toward the full-looking marmot, who bolted and left a trail of dropped stew ingredients. Griselda let out a hearty huff of laughter that shook her frame. “A marmot. Well, I’ll be dipped in lava.”

Boggle held Glimmer toward Reginald. As its light intensified, a soft warm glow came from the case. Reginald fumbled the latch. On dark velvet lay the Lumina-Fiddle. “Oh dear. It seems my admirer was quite attached to its music. Perhaps a simple arrangement for borrowing would have sufficed.” He beamed. Glimmer pulsed, pleased.

Then the pots. Boggle directed Mort to a slightly loose floorboard near the hearth and handed him a small intricately carved wooden spring from his satchel — a forgotten piece of gadget. Mort, doubtful but desperate, fitted it into a tiny mechanism. The thrumming stopped. The pots settled. A simple device for regulating heat vents: unbalanced, it had made the stone floor dance.

The inn buzzed, then laughed. Griselda clapped Boggle on the back, nearly sending him flying. “You’ve untangled our knots.” Reginald offered to let Glimmer listen anytime. The marmot, full and pleased, was declared honorary mascot, to Griselda’s grudging amusement.

Boggle stood a moment in the steam and the leftover clatter, Glimmer cool in his arms, Moss leaning against his patched shin. He had come for moss that mended roofs. He had found a creature that mended mornings. The Crags would wait. The vents would stay balanced, if Mort remembered the spring.

That evening, in the cozy dwelling beneath ash-dusted peaks, Boggle, Moss, and Glimmer shared roasted roots and sweet berry juice. The roof still needed moss. The spring still hummed. Glimmer’s light lay on the patched tunic like a second mending. Boggle did not name what he had found. He only set a spare bowl where moonlight could reach it, and Moss curled against the star-spun warmth, and the Ashlands kept their twilight, a little less bare than dawn. Outside, the grey meadows held their quiet. Inside, three kinds of shine — ferret, goblin gadget-spring, moonbeam — shared the same small room, and that was enough of a patch for one day.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
